stem: A 35-year-old man presents for evaluation of fatigue. Laboratory tests reveal a microcytic anemia with a normal red cell distribution width (RDW) and normal ferritin levels. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely cause of his anemia?
stemHtml: A 35-year-old man presents for evaluation of fatigue. Laboratory tests reveal a microcytic anemia with a normal red cell distribution width (RDW) and normal ferritin levels. Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely cause of his anemia? (Question Id: 501021)
keywords: Microcytic anemia – indicates small RBCs, narrows differential to microcytic anemias.
Normal RDW – classic clue for thalassemia minor, as all RBCs are uniformly small.
Normal ferritin – rules out iron deficiency anemia.
keywordsHtml:
1. Microcytic anemia – indicates small RBCs, narrows differential to microcytic anemias.
  2. Normal RDW – classic clue for thalassemia minor, as all RBCs are uniformly small.
  3. Normal ferritin – rules out iron deficiency anemia.

B.title: Beta-thalassemia minor
B.body:
β-thalassemia minor is a hereditary microcytic anemia caused by a partial defect in the synthesis of the β-globin chain of hemoglobin.
This results in small (microcytic) red blood cells (low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)). Critically, the body produces a large number of uniformly small cells, which is why the Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW)—a measure of the variation in red cell size—is typically normal.
Furthermore, since the anemia is not due to iron depletion, the ferritin level (which reflects iron stores) is normal.
This combination of microcytosis, normal RDW, and normal ferritin is the classic hematological pattern for β -thalassemia minor.
Often mild and asymptomatic, may be discovered incidentally.
Peripheral smear may show target cells and basophilic stippling.
Key lab clue: MCV is low out of proportion to mild anemia.
B.bodyHtml:
• β-thalassemia minor is a hereditary microcytic anemia caused by a partial defect in the synthesis of the β-globin chain of hemoglobin.
  • This results in small (microcytic) red blood cells (low Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)). Critically, the body produces a large number of uniformly small cells, which is why the Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW)—a measure of the variation in red cell size—is typically normal.
  • Furthermore, since the anemia is not due to iron depletion, the ferritin level (which reflects iron stores) is normal.
  • This combination of microcytosis, normal RDW, and normal ferritin is the classic hematological pattern for β -thalassemia minor.
  • Often mild and asymptomatic, may be discovered incidentally.
  • Peripheral smear may show target cells and basophilic stippling.
  • Key lab clue: MCV is low out of proportion to mild anemia.

A.title: Iron deficiency anemia
A.body:
Usually presents with microcytic, hypochromic anemia, but RDW is typically elevated due to mixed populations of small and normal RBCs.
Ferritin is low in iron deficiency, which helps differentiate it from thalassemia.
Not consistent with normal RDW and normal ferritin.
A.bodyHtml:
• Usually presents with microcytic, hypochromic anemia, but RDW is typically elevated due to mixed populations of small and normal RBCs.
  • Ferritin is low in iron deficiency, which helps differentiate it from thalassemia.
  • Not consistent with normal RDW and normal ferritin.

C.title: Anemia of chronic disease
C.body:
Usually normocytic, sometimes mildly microcytic.
Ferritin is normal or elevated (acute phase reactant), but anemia is usually mild.
RDW is usually normal.
Often associated with chronic infection, inflammation, or malignancy.
C.bodyHtml:
• Usually normocytic, sometimes mildly microcytic.
  • Ferritin is normal or elevated (acute phase reactant), but anemia is usually mild.
  • RDW is usually normal.
  • Often associated with chronic infection, inflammation, or malignancy.

D.title: Lead poisoning
D.body:
Can cause microcytic anemia, sometimes with basophilic stippling.
RDW may be slightly elevated.
Often associated with neurological symptoms or exposure history.
Ferritin is usually normal.
D.bodyHtml:
• Can cause microcytic anemia, sometimes with basophilic stippling.
  • RDW may be slightly elevated.
  • Often associated with neurological symptoms or exposure history.
  • Ferritin is usually normal.

E.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency
E.body:
Causes macrocytic anemia, not microcytic.
RDW is often elevated due to mixed cell populations.
Peripheral smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils.
E.bodyHtml:
• Causes macrocytic anemia, not microcytic.
  • RDW is often elevated due to mixed cell populations.
  • Peripheral smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils.

keyConcept:
Microcytic anemia with normal RDW and normal ferritin → think thalassemia minor.
Iron deficiency anemia usually has low ferritin and high RDW.
Beta-thalassemia minor produces uniformly small RBCs due to a genetic globin defect, not iron deficiency.
keyConceptHtml:
• Microcytic anemia with normal RDW and normal ferritin → think thalassemia minor.
  • Iron deficiency anemia usually has low ferritin and high RDW.
  • Beta-thalassemia minor produces uniformly small RBCs due to a genetic globin defect, not iron deficiency.
classicTriad: Microcytosis + Normal RDW + Normal Ferritin → highly suggestive of beta-thalassemia minor.
